How a web app works

When a user accesses a web application, the browser retrieves and executes the frontend files from the Web Server. As the user interacts with the application—such as viewing data—the frontend initiates an API request. This request is sent to the backend over HTTPS, and the backend processes it to return a response. If the user uploads a file (e.g., a PDF), the backend stores the physical file in a shared folder on a Samba File Server and saves only the file's path in the database alongside the relevant record.

Browser
Downloads and runs the frontend files, then sends API requests initiated by the frontend.
Web Server
Serves the frontend build, including the HTML, JavaScript, and CSS files that the browser needs.
Application Server
Runs the backend API. For a course list request, it returns the course data and can read it from Redis or PostgreSQL.
Cache Server
Redis can temporarily store results such as a course list. The backend can return a cached result when available. On a cache miss, it can query PostgreSQL and cache the new result for a limited time.
Database Server
Runs PostgreSQL, which executes SQL and manages records such as courses and enrollments. PostgreSQL keeps its data files on persistent storage so the records remain after the server process restarts.
File Server
Samba is the file server software in this example. It shares a folder over SMB so the backend can write uploaded PDFs and read them again for downloads.
